bib.title: Adapting While Learning: Grounding LLMs for Scientific Problems with Tool Usage Adaptation
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025 (arXiv v4, 20 Jun 2025)

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only for lineage; figure images not viewed (bar-chart values only where printed as text).

question: How can an LLM be fine-tuned to solve scientific problems accurately while deciding adaptively, per problem, whether to answer directly or call a scientific tool?
hypothesis: Models fine-tuned on tool usage over-rely on tools; training them to internalise tool-derived knowledge and to use tools only on problems they cannot solve directly will raise accuracy and tool-decision quality at lower tool cost.
contributions: A two-component training paradigm, Adapting While Learning (AWL): World Knowledge Learning (WKL) and Tool Usage Adaptation (TUA).
Four new datasets spanning epidemiology, climate, Mujoco and PDEs.
Average improvement of 29.11% in answer accuracy and 12.72% in tool usage accuracy over the base model; surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 on the new custom datasets.

method.summary: Tool-using traces are generated for each training question with a forced-tool prompt Pf; a solution y is written from the tool outputs. WKL fine-tunes the model to produce y directly with no tools (prompt Pn). TUA partitions questions into easy/hard by the model's own direct-answer accuracy and trains direct answers on easy ones and tool traces on hard ones under one prompt Pi, so the model learns to decide implicitly. A combined loss J_Mix = J_WKL + J_TUA is optimised, partitioning at the start of each epoch; open-ended questions add a DPO term over ranked proposals.
method.task: Scientific question answering (multiple choice and numerical) and open-ended design/planning, with adaptive tool-use decisions

datasets.name: Mujoco (custom)
datasets.source: Built by the authors on the Mujoco physics engine from 8 scenario types; average 14.5 adjustable parameters per scenario
datasets.preprocessing: Templates filled by sampling parameters in valid ranges; answers precomputed with the simulator

datasets.name: Climate (custom) multi-choice
datasets.source: Neural surrogate model (Niu et al., 2024); 12 climate driver variables, ssp126/245/370/585

datasets.name: Epidemiology (custom) multi-choice
datasets.source: Surrogate model (Wu et al., 2023), California, 58 counties

datasets.name: MATH
datasets.split: standard configuration; test problems with definite numerical answers

datasets.name: SciBench
datasets.split: random split by the authors (no official train set)

datasets.name: Climate open-ended
datasets.source: Maritime route design with neural climate surrogate

datasets.name: Epidemiology open-ended
datasets.source: Intervention budget allocation with epidemic surrogate

other.note: scalability check on PDE, Mujoco, MATH, SciBench only

other.use: labels error types in Section 5.4 / Appendix G

training.objective: Combined loss J_Mix = J_WKL + J_TUA (Eq. 6): negative log-likelihood of tool-derived solution y under no-tool prompt Pn (WKL), plus NLL of y on easy questions and of the tool trace t on hard questions under Pi (TUA). Open-ended questions add a DPO loss on preference pairs from ranked proposals.
training.regularisation: LoRA for DPO: target all, rank 8, DPO beta 0.1
training.hardware: L40S and A100 servers (counts not stated)

other.iterations: two iterations of AWL training in the main experiments
other.partition_timing: easy/hard partition recomputed at the start of each epoch
other.partition_rule_mcq: sample an ensemble of direct answers; easy if accuracy exceeds a predefined threshold (threshold value not given); sensitivity to ensemble size k = 1, 3 and 5 in Table 6
other.partition_rule_open_ended: easy if proposals meet the thresholds in at least 4 of 5 attempts under Pi
other.open_ended_dpo_recipe: SFT on preferred answers first, then LoRA DPO
other.open_ended_acceptance: climate: route raises global mean temperature by at most 0.01 C; epidemiology: indicator below 0.1
other.open_ended_tool_budgets: climate: at most 5 uses of the validity tool and 3 of the quantitative tool; epidemiology: one integrated tool, at most 3 uses

inference.samples: not stated for evaluation; k = 1, 3, and 5 samples used in the difficulty-threshold sensitivity study
inference.prompting: Four prompts: Pn (no tools, Solution/Answer format), Pi (tool or direct answer, JSON function call for custom datasets; Thought/Action/Code format for MATH and SciBench), Pf (Pi with the adaptive-use wording removed, forces tool use), and Pi with ICL (few examples of correct tool-use decisions).

other.tools: Mujoco scenario APIs; in-house PDE solvers; neural surrogate APIs for climate and epidemiology; SymPy and NumPy scripts (write_and_run_code) for MATH and SciBench; an answer_question tool is used to standardise answers
other.inference_deployment: open-source models served internally; proprietary models via API

metrics.name: Answer accuracy
metrics.definition: Share of correct answers. MCQ: binary on chosen option; MATH: prior math-specific evaluation (Yang et al., 2024); SciBench: correct if within +-5% of true value.

metrics.name: Tool usage accuracy
metrics.definition: 1/2 x (EN/(EN+ET) + HT/(HN+HT)); questions are easy (E) or hard (H) by the model's no-tool (Pn) accuracy; with Pi the model uses a tool (T) or not (N). 50% means random decisions.

metrics.name: Open-ended success
metrics.definition: Percentage of proposals meeting the constraints and a pre-established quality threshold

metrics.name: Pairwise win rate
metrics.definition: Percentage of open-ended questions on which one model's proposal beats another's (Fig. 16)

baselines: Llama3.1-8B base with Pn, Pi, Pf, and ICL
w/o WKL and w/o TUA ablations
eval.protocol: Single table value per cell; no seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests reported. Test sets are small (80 to 280 questions). Error types annotated by GPT-4o.

availability.data: Four new datasets released per the contribution claim; no explicit URL beyond the code repository

<Your code>

If you want to answer the question, you should answer in the following format:

Action: answer_question
Solution: <Your solution>

Question: {{question}}

I will give you a question, along with its correct solution and an incorrect solution. Please analyze the reason for the mistake. The reason for the mistake should be chosen from the following three categories: 1. Calculation mistakes, 2. Logical Reasoning errors, 3. Knowledge gaps. If the mistake does not fall into any of these categories, please suggest what you think is the correct category. Calculation mistakes are mistakes that arise from incorrect calculations. Logic Reasoning errors are caused by errors from abstract causal reasoning. Knowledge gaps are mistakes that arise from a lack of knowledge, including misinterpretation of concepts or lack of understanding of the question, and incorrect reasoning caused by a misunderstanding of scientific knowledge. Your answer should be in the following format:
Thought: [Your analysis]
Category: [The category you choose]

evidence.where: Table 9: full-parameter SFT 1.0e-5; DPO with LoRA 5.0e-6

evidence.quote: In the main experiments, we performed two iterations of AWL training.

results.claim: AWL raises average answer accuracy of Llama-3.1-8B by 29.11 points (no-tool Pn vs base Pn, per the Table 1 averages 59.31 vs 30.20).
results.metric: Answer accuracy gain, average over 6 datasets
results.setup: Llama3.1-8B-AWL-Pn vs Llama3.1-8B (Base)-Pn on Mujoco, PDE, Climate, Epidemiology, MATH, SciBench; one run, no variance.
results.quote: post-trained with AWL achieve 29.11% higher answer accuracy and 12.72% better tool usage accuracy
results.note: Abstract wording says 'higher', unit ambiguous; the table averages (59.31 minus 30.20 = 29.11) show it is percentage points on the no-tool prompts. Versus base Pi (56.16) the AWL-Pi gain is 9.97 points.

results.claim: Tool usage accuracy of AWL averages 63.93% versus 51.21% for the base model (12.72 points), while GPT-4o, Claude-3.5 and Llama-70B sit near 50%, i.e. random decisions.
results.setup: Six datasets, Table 2; frontier models average 49.28 to 54.68.
results.table: Table 2, row Llama3.1-8B-AWL, column Average (63.93); row Llama3.1-8B (Base), column Average (51.21)

results.claim: Full AWL (Pi) averages 66.13% answer accuracy, above GPT-4o at 57.50% and Llama3.1-70B at 48.25%, although the gap is mainly on the custom datasets.
results.setup: Table 1, six datasets, Llama3.1-8B-AWL-Pi vs GPT4o.
results.table: Table 1, row Llama3.1-8B-AWL-Pi, column Average (66.13); row GPT4o, column Average (57.50)
results.note: On MATH and SciBench GPT4o scores 82.94 and 71.67 versus AWL-Pi 62.35 and 34.17; the paper concedes frontier models beat AWL on public data.

results.claim: Epidemiology is the largest single gain: AWL-Pi reaches 74.44% against 18.89% for base Pn and 32.50% for GPT4o.
results.table: Table 1, row Llama3.1-8B-AWL-Pi, column Epidemiology (74.44); row Llama3.1-8B (Base)-Pn, column Epidemiology (18.89)

results.claim: Forcing the base model to use tools (Pf) already lifts average accuracy from 30.20% to 57.60%, so much of the AWL gain on custom datasets is what tool access alone provides; AWL-Pn (no tools) matches this at 59.31%.
results.setup: Llama3.1-8B base, Pf vs Pn, six datasets.

results.claim: The base model almost always calls tools regardless of difficulty: average tool usage rate 90.96% versus 51.72% for AWL.
results.metric: Tool usage rate, average (lower is better)
results.table: Table 16, row Llama3.1-8B-AWL, column Average (51.72); row Llama3.1-8B (Base), column Average (90.96)

results.claim: On open-ended questions AWL cuts the mean tool calls per question from 7.21 to 2.70 on Climate and from 2.80 to 0.42 on Epidemiology without hurting output quality.
results.setup: Open-ended Climate (120 test) and Epidemiology (80 test); base vs AWL-RL.
results.quote: our method reduces the average call to tools per question from 7.21 to 2.70 in Climate tasks and from 2.80 to 0.42 in Epidemiology tasks

results.claim: On open-ended Epidemiology, AWL-RL-Pi satisfies the constraints in 56.25% of cases versus 17.50% for the base model, 43.75% for GPT4o and 36.25% for Claude3.5.
results.table: Table 4, row Epidemiology, column AWL-RL-Pi (56.25); column Base (17.50)

results.claim: Scalability check: post-training Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct lifts MATH answer accuracy from 74.12% to 81.18% without tools (Pn), and SciBench from 17.50% to 56.67%.
results.table: Table 3, row Ans Acc. AWL-Pn, column MATH (81.18); row Ans Acc. Base-Pn (74.12)

results.claim: Tool usage accuracy for Qwen2.5-14B after AWL stays modest (54.16 to 63.58%), so the adaptive decision is only partly learned at 14B.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-14B on Mujoco (lowest of the four).
results.table: Table 3, row Tool Usage Acc. AWL, column Mujoco (54.16); row Tool Usage Acc. Base, column Mujoco (50.00)

results.claim: Ablation: omitting either WKL or TUA produces tool over-reliance, and without WKL answer accuracy is lowest.
results.setup: Climate and PDE datasets, Fig. 6 (bar proportions not printed as text).

results.claim: With noisy training labels, SFT-only accuracy on the Climate dataset drops while AWL holds up because the model judges polluted questions hard and uses tools.
results.setup: Climate and PDE, noise 0 to 100%, Fig. 7; values read from the figure only.
results.note: Values appear in the figure text (e.g. 0.93, 0.89 for the first points) but the series assignment is not recoverable from the extracted text.

results.claim: After AWL the dominant remaining error is agent limitation (e.g. 80.00% of PDE errors), not knowledge gaps; absolute counts fall in every category.
results.metric: Share of errors that are agent limitation, PDE
results.setup: GPT-4o-annotated errors of the no-tool (Pn) model, Table 7; absolute counts in Table 17.
results.table: Table 7, block AWL, row Agent Limitation, column PDE (80.00); block Base Model (61.05)
results.note: The annotator is GPT-4o with no stated validation against humans.

results.claim: Closed frontier models over-rely on tools for the custom datasets but answer directly on public ones, which the authors read as evidence of pretraining exposure.
results.setup: Fig. 15, MATH vs PDE composition of tool decisions; also Claude-3.5 tool rate on MATH is 10.59% (Table 16).
results.note: The contamination explanation is a hypothesis, not tested.

limits: Requires domain-specific fine-tuning per domain; unified training across domains is future work (Section 6).
Difficulty is a binary easy/hard split from the model's own sampled accuracy; real problems lie on a spectrum.
The easy/hard threshold for multi-choice partition is not stated (only the 4-of-5 rule for open-ended); k=1,3,5 sensitivity only on MATH and SciBench.
Decision is made once per question, not stepwise within multi-step workflows.
On public benchmarks the 8B model stays below GPT4o and Claude (MATH 62.35 vs 82.94; SciBench 34.17 vs 71.67), which the authors attribute to pretraining coverage and model size, untested.

Most custom-data gains are comparable to simply forcing tool use (Pf 57.60 vs AWL-Pn 59.31 average), so the benefit is internalising tool knowledge and cutting tool calls rather than raising accuracy over tool use.
The custom datasets are template-generated from the same simulators used as tools, so train/test share templates; generalisation beyond the templates is not tested.
No seeds, variance or significance tests; test sets are 80 to 280 questions; decoding settings, optimiser and GPU counts not stated.
Tool usage accuracy is defined relative to the model's own no-tool accuracy, so the label changes per model and is not comparable across models.
Error-type annotation relies on GPT-4o without human check.

terms.definition: Supervised fine-tuning (and DPO for open-ended questions) of a model to produce tool-derived solutions directly, internalising scientific knowledge.
Classify problems as easy or hard from the model's accuracy; keep direct-answer targets for easy ones and switch targets to tool-usage traces for hard ones.
